claim_verdicts.slide: The Data Science Hierarchy of Needs
claim_verdicts.bullet: A 2016 CrowdFlower survey found that data scientists spend roughly 80% of their time on data preparation: 60% cleaning and organizing data, 19% collecting datasets
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Almost the same percentage of respondents reported they spent most of their time cleaning data (60 percent) as those who reported that task to be the least enjoyable part of their job (57 percent). An additional 19 percent of time was reported spent on collecting data sets, bringing the total data preparation effort to approximately 79 percent.

claim_verdicts.slide: What Is Training-Serving Skew?
claim_verdicts.bullet: Training-serving skew is a difference between performance during training and during serving, caused by: (1) divergent data handling in training vs. serving pipelines, (2) data changes between training and serving time, or (3) feedback loops between model and algorithm
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Training-serving skew is a difference between performance during training and performance during serving. This skew can be caused by: A discrepancy between how you handle data in the training and serving pipelines. A change in the data between when you train and when you serve. A feedback loop between your model and your algorithm.

claim_verdicts.slide: What Is Training-Serving Skew?
claim_verdicts.bullet: Prevention: log the features used at serving time and replay them during training to verify consistency between the two environments
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: The best way to make sure that you train like you serve is to save the set of features used at serving time, and then pipe those features to a log to use them at training time. Even if you can't do this for every example, do it for a small fraction, such that you can verify the consistency between serving and training.

claim_verdicts.slide: Temporal Leakage — The Naive Join Trap
claim_verdicts.bullet: Temporal leakage occurs when a naive join uses current or future feature values instead of the values available at prediction time, producing over-optimistic offline metrics that do not generalize to production
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Feature values in Feast are modeled as time-series records. Feast is able to join features from one or more feature views onto an entity dataframe in a point-in-time correct way. This means Feast is able to reproduce the state of features at a specific point in the past. Feast joins these tables with battle-tested logic that ensures point-in-time correctness so future feature values do not leak to models.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source establishes that point-in-time joins prevent future feature values from leaking, confirming the mechanism of temporal leakage. However, the consequence stated in the bullet — 'producing over-optimistic offline metrics that do not generalize to production' — is not mentioned in the Feast source. The source describes the fix (point-in-time correctness), not the downstream harm of the leakage.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Temporal leakage occurs when a naive join uses current or future feature values instead of the values available at prediction time; point-in-time correct joins prevent future feature values from leaking into training data.

claim_verdicts.slide: Temporal Leakage — The Naive Join Trap
claim_verdicts.bullet: In the transactions/customer/labels schema, a join on customer_id without a timestamp constraint attaches post-event attributes (e.g., a credit limit increased after the label was recorded) to training rows, giving the model access to information unavailable at prediction time
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: A point-in-time correct join is a temporal join between two tables where the output reflects the state of both tables at a specific point in time defined by timestamps from the left table. In SQL, a PiT Join is an ASOF LEFT JOIN. The AS OF join ensures that the most recent value of the feature at the time of the timestamp is used in the training set.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source defines point-in-time correct joins in general terms but does not mention the transactions/customer/labels schema, the credit_limit attribute, or the specific scenario of a post-event attribute update. The bullet presents a concrete example as if it is sourced from the cited document, but the specific schema and example are not in the source.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: A join on a slowly-changing dimension without a timestamp constraint returns the current value of attributes rather than the value at the time of the label event, giving the model access to information unavailable at prediction time; a point-in-time correct join retrieves the most recent value of each feature at or before the label timestamp.

claim_verdicts.slide: Skew vs. Drift — Don't Conflate Them
claim_verdicts.bullet: Consistency mismatch between training and serving code paths [claim:agentic-de:011] (What row)
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: TensorFlow Data Validation can detect distribution skew between training and serving data. Distribution skew occurs when the distribution of feature values for training data is significantly different from serving data. One of the key causes for distribution skew is using either a completely different corpus for training data generation to overcome lack of initial data in the desired corpus. Another reason is a faulty sampling mechanism that only chooses a subsample of the serving data to train on.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source describes training-serving skew as a difference in feature value distributions between training and serving data, attributing it to different corpora or faulty sampling. The bullet frames it as a 'consistency mismatch between training and serving code paths,' which is a different (and narrower) cause-based framing not stated in the TFDV source. The source does not use the term 'code paths.'
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Training-serving skew: a difference in feature value distributions between training and serving data, caused by using different corpora or faulty sampling mechanisms that select only a subsample of serving data for training.

claim_verdicts.slide: Skew vs. Drift — Don't Conflate Them
claim_verdicts.bullet: Change in the joint probability distribution P(X, Y) over time [claim:agentic-de:012] (What row)
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: In predictive analytics, data science, machine learning and related fields, concept drift is an evolution of data that invalidates the data model. It happens when the statistical properties of the target variable, which the model is trying to predict, change over time in unforeseen ways. Formal definition: Concept drift is a change in the joint probability distribution P(X,Y) between two time instances t and t+w.

claim_verdicts.slide: Reproducibility as a Three-Layer Temporal Problem
claim_verdicts.bullet: ML reproducibility requires pinning three layers to the same point in time: the data state (lakehouse snapshots or content-addressed versions), the code/pipeline state (Git commits), and the embedding-model version (checkpoint or API version)
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: A multi-level versioning system addresses managing changes to various components while preserving result comparability through task versioning where each version maintains its own evaluation protocol, dataset versioning where each dataset references a specific revision from its source ensuring identical data across evaluation runs, and model versioning where models reference specific checkpoints or API versions to maintain consistency.
claim_verdicts.issue: The bullet maps the source's three versioning types onto different concepts: (1) 'task versioning (evaluation protocol)' is rephrased as 'code/pipeline state (Git commits),' which is a different concept entirely — the MTEB source is about evaluation task protocols for benchmarks, not code versioning via Git; (2) 'lakehouse snapshots or content-addressed versions' for the data layer are not mentioned in the source; (3) the source is specifically about embedding benchmark reproducibility (MTEB), not general ML pipeline reproducibility. The bullet extrapolates the framing far beyond what the cited source supports.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: ML reproducibility requires versioning three components: the dataset (each dataset references a specific revision to ensure identical data across runs), the evaluation/task protocol (each task version maintains its own evaluation protocol), and the model (models reference specific checkpoints or API versions). [Note: source is specific to embedding benchmarks; expand citation or reframe to match source scope.]

claim_verdicts.slide: Reproducibility as a Three-Layer Temporal Problem
claim_verdicts.bullet: Without coupling all three layers, re-running a pipeline on 'the same data' can produce different results if the embedding model has changed
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: A multi-level versioning system addresses managing changes to various components while preserving result comparability through task versioning where each version maintains its own evaluation protocol, dataset versioning where each dataset references a specific revision from its source ensuring identical data across evaluation runs, and model versioning where models reference specific checkpoints or API versions to maintain consistency.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source says model versioning ensures consistency by referencing specific checkpoints or API versions, implying that without it results could differ — but it does not explicitly state that 're-running a pipeline on the same data can produce different results if the embedding model has changed.' The source is about benchmark evaluation reproducibility (MTEB), not general ML pipeline re-execution. The bullet's causal phrasing is a reasonable inference but goes beyond what the source text states.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Without versioning all three components, result comparability is lost: changing any of task protocol, dataset revision, or model checkpoint/API version will produce different results even when the other components appear identical.

claim_verdicts.slide: Lakehouse Time Travel — Delta Lake and Iceberg
claim_verdicts.bullet: Delta Lake: time travel via VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF queries; the default VACUUM retention period is 7 days (delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration), so time travel beyond 7 days requires explicitly increasing retention at the cost of additional storage
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: The default retention threshold for data files after running VACUUM is 7 days. The retention window for the VACUUM command is determined by the delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration table property, which defaults to 7 days. This means VACUUM removes data files that are no longer referenced by a Delta table version in the last 7 days. The default configuration for VACUUM deletes stale data files that are older than seven days. As a result, if you run VACUUM with the default settings, you will only be able to time travel seven days into the past.

claim_verdicts.slide: Lakehouse Time Travel — Delta Lake and Iceberg
claim_verdicts.bullet: Apache Iceberg: every write creates a new immutable snapshot referencing manifest lists and data files; time-travel queries follow older snapshot pointers, but even small data changes create new versions of data and metadata files, increasing storage usage; over time snapshot accumulation also causes metadata bloat
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Even small changes in the data can result in the creation of new versions of data and metadata files. Storing multiple snapshots and versions of data files increases the storage usage. Over the period, snapshots accumulate, and metadata files grow larger. The content of metadata files becomes complex, hence it increases memory requirements for query planning.

claim_verdicts.slide: Content-Addressable Versioning — DVC and lakeFS
claim_verdicts.bullet: DVC: uses content-addressable storage with MD5 hashes to deduplicate data; files are stored in a cache keyed by hash, and lightweight .dvc metafiles tracked in Git link each commit to an exact dataset state without storing large files in the repository
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: The cache uses content-addressable storage, meaning files are stored based on their hash. This prevents data duplication; if you have multiple copies of the same file (even with different names or locations), DVC stores only one copy in the cache. DVC calculates the file hash, a 32 characters long string (usually MD5). The first two characters are used to name the directory inside the cache, and the rest become the file name of the cached file. Instead of storing large files directly in your Git repository, DVC stores lightweight metadata files (called .dvc files) that act as pointers to the actual data. These .dvc files are tracked by Git. Since the metafile is versioned by Git, DVC ties data to specific code versions.

claim_verdicts.slide: Content-Addressable Versioning — DVC and lakeFS
claim_verdicts.bullet: lakeFS: provides Git-like version control (branches, commits, merges) over object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) using zero-copy branching — creating a branch is a metadata-only operation with no data duplication; storage overhead only occurs when data is actually modified on a branch
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Branches are simply a pointer to a commit along with a set of uncommitted changes, and creating a branch is a zero-copy operation where instead of duplicating data, it involves creating a pointer to the source commit for the branch. The actual data itself is not stored inside lakeFS directly but in an underlying object store. lakeFS supports managing data in AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, and any other object storage with an S3 interface.

claim_verdicts.slide: Three Kinds of Drift
claim_verdicts.bullet: Schema drift — a structural change such as a missing column or type mismatch; breaks pipelines visibly
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: The fourth concern is that the schema that your features follow can change over time. If you don't have a way to version your schemas and map each of your features to its expected schema, the cause of the reported alert might be due to the mismatched schema rather than a change in the data.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source mentions schema changes as a concern but does not say schema drift 'breaks pipelines visibly.' The source actually describes schema drift as a cause of alerts that might be misdiagnosed — implying it surfaces through monitoring, not necessarily as a visible pipeline break. The characterization 'breaks pipelines visibly' is not in the source.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Schema drift — a structural change such as a mismatched schema in your features over time; can cause monitoring alerts that may be misattributed to data distribution changes rather than schema changes.

claim_verdicts.slide: Three Kinds of Drift
claim_verdicts.bullet: Distribution drift (covariate shift) — P(X) changes but P(Y|X) stays the same; degrades models silently
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Covariate shift: P(X) changes, but P(Y|X) remains the same. This refers to the first decomposition of the joint distribution.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source directly supports 'P(X) changes but P(Y|X) remains the same.' However, 'degrades models silently' is not stated in the source. The source describes the definition of covariate shift only, not its operational impact on model quality or its detectability.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Distribution drift (covariate shift) — P(X) changes but P(Y|X) remains the same.

claim_verdicts.slide: Three Kinds of Drift
claim_verdicts.bullet: Concept drift — P(Y|X) changes but P(X) stays the same; the learned relationship between inputs and outputs shifts
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Concept drift: P(Y|X) changes, but P(X) remains the same. This refers to the first decomposition of the joint distribution.
